body:
The Rashtrakutas and their geographical base

The Rashtrakutas were an important ruling dynasty of early-medieval India. Their imperial power emerged in the western Deccan during the middle of the 8th century CE and continued until the late 10th century CE. The Deccan is the plateau region of peninsular India, and the principal Rashtrakuta territories included parts of present-day Maharashtra and Karnataka.

The Rashtrakutas are important for 3 connected reasons. They established a powerful kingdom after overthrowing their former overlords, participated in political struggles extending into northern India, and supported major architectural works, especially the Kailasa temple at Ellora. Their territories also had commercial connections with the western coast and overseas traders.

How a subordinate chief became an independent ruler

During the early-medieval period, powerful kings often depended on regional chiefs known as samantas. A samanta acknowledged the authority of a stronger ruler and was generally expected to attend the overlord's court, present gifts and provide military assistance. In return, the chief could retain influence within a particular region.

Such an arrangement was not necessarily permanent. When a samanta accumulated sufficient military strength and resources, he could challenge the overlord and establish an independent kingdom.

The Rashtrakutas provide a clear example. They were initially subordinate to the Chalukyas of Karnataka, commonly called the Chalukyas of Badami or early Western Chalukyas. In the middle of the 8th century CE, the Rashtrakuta chief Dantidurga defeated his Chalukya overlord and established independent Rashtrakuta power. The overthrow is generally placed around 753–754 CE.

Dantidurga is associated with the establishment of independent Rashtrakuta imperial rule. The dynasty that he displaced was the Chalukya dynasty of Badami.

The hiranyagarbha ritual and political legitimacy

Dantidurga is also associated with the ritual called hiranyagarbha, literally meaning golden womb. According to the account described in early-medieval history, Brahmanas performed this ritual, which symbolically represented the rebirth of its patron as a Kshatriya.

The political significance is more important than the literal meaning. A ruler who had gained power through military success also sought recognition as a legitimate king within the prevailing social and religious order. Performing the ritual helped express that claim.

The ritual should not be treated as evidence that Dantidurga acquired his kingdom through a religious ceremony. Military success established his political independence; the ritual expressed and strengthened his claim to royal status.

Manyakheta: the political centre

The Rashtrakuta imperial capital became closely associated with Manyakheta, also called Malkhed, in present-day Karnataka. Manyakheta developed into a major royal centre particularly under Amoghavarsha I in the 9th century CE.

Several places connected with the Rashtrakutas had different functions:

  • Western Deccan: the principal territorial base of imperial Rashtrakuta power.
  • Manyakheta: an important political and administrative capital.
  • Ellora: a major religious and artistic site, especially associated with the Kailasa temple.
  • Kanauj: a northern Indian city contested by the Rashtrakutas and other powerful dynasties.

These distinctions matter because a dynasty could have its capital in one place, sponsor a temple elsewhere, and conduct military campaigns in still another region.

How the kingdom supported its activities

Early-medieval rulers obtained resources from agricultural producers, artisans and traders. Revenue helped maintain royal establishments and armies, while land grants, temples and military campaigns also formed part of political life. Control over productive land and access to trade routes increased the resources available to competing kingdoms.

For the Rashtrakutas, their Deccan base connected inland political power with routes leading towards the western coast. This relationship helps explain why trade and accounts by merchants from West Asia form part of the history of the dynasty.

Prelims focus

  • The Rashtrakutas rose to imperial power in the western Deccan in the middle of the 8th century CE.
  • Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami around 753–754 CE.
  • Samantas were subordinate chiefs who could become independent rulers.
  • Hiranyagarbha means golden womb and symbolised a claim to Kshatriya status.
  • Manyakheta or Malkhed, in present-day Karnataka, was an important Rashtrakuta capital.
  • Trap: Ellora was an important Rashtrakuta-period temple site, not the imperial capital.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, printed pp. 16–18; IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 to 1206, BHIC-132, Unit 10, Emergence of Rashtrakutas, printed pp. 152–156, 2019.]

body:
Why the rulers must be distinguished

The Rashtrakuta dynasty lasted for more than 2 centuries. Different rulers are remembered for different achievements: establishing independence, extending military influence, supporting learning or building temples. Matching each ruler with the correct achievement is more useful than treating the entire period as the work of a single king.

Important rulers and their principal associations

RulerPeriodMain association
DantidurgaMiddle of the 8th century CEOverthrew the Chalukya overlord and established independent Rashtrakuta power.
Krishna ILater 8th century CETraditionally credited with the Kailasa temple, Cave 16, at Ellora.
DhruvaLate 8th century CEExtended Rashtrakuta military influence into northern India.
Govinda IIIEarly 9th century CEConducted major military campaigns in northern and southern India.
Amoghavarsha Ic. 814–878 CEAssociated with Manyakheta and the Kannada literary work Kavirajamarga.
Indra IIIEarly 10th century CEConducted a successful northern campaign against the Gurjara-Pratiharas and attacked Kanauj.
Krishna IIIMiddle of the 10th century CEDefeated Chola forces at the Battle of Takkolam, generally dated to c. 949 CE.
Karka II973 CEWas overthrown by Tailapa II, marking the end of imperial Rashtrakuta rule in the Deccan.

Krishna I and Krishna III must not be confused. Krishna I is associated with the construction of the Kailasa temple at Ellora, while Krishna III is associated with later military campaigns against the Cholas.

Likewise, Amoghavarsha I is especially associated with literature and the royal centre at Manyakheta. The Kavirajamarga, an important early work on Kannada language and poetics, is associated with his reign and patronage.

What was the tripartite struggle?

The tripartite struggle was a prolonged contest among 3 major dynasties for influence over Kanauj, an important city in the Ganga valley of northern India.

DynastyMain regional baseRole in the struggle
RashtrakutasDeccanSent armies northward to challenge rival powers.
Gurjara-PratiharasWestern and northern IndiaCompeted for control of Kanauj and the surrounding region.
PalasBengal and adjoining eastern regionsExtended their ambitions towards Kanauj from the east.

Kanauj was valuable because of its strategic position in the fertile Ganga valley and the prestige associated with controlling a prominent northern Indian political centre. Military success in the region could strengthen a ruler's claim to wider authority.

However, winning a campaign did not necessarily mean permanently annexing the region. The balance of power changed over time. The Rashtrakutas could defeat rivals in northern India without relocating their permanent political base from the Deccan.

The Rashtrakutas, Palas and Gurjara-Pratiharas were the 3 parties in the tripartite struggle. Kanauj was the object of the contest, not the original capital of all 3 dynasties.

Decline and replacement of Rashtrakuta power

Krishna III was among the last major Rashtrakuta rulers. His victory over Chola forces at Takkolam, around 949 CE, demonstrated that the dynasty remained a significant military power in the middle of the 10th century.

Rashtrakuta imperial rule nevertheless ended a few decades later. Around 973 CE, Tailapa II defeated the Rashtrakuta ruler Karka II and established the power of the later Western Chalukyas, also known as the Chalukyas of Kalyani.

This creates an important chronological distinction: the Rashtrakutas initially displaced the early Western Chalukyas of Badami in the 8th century, but their own imperial power was later displaced by the Western Chalukyas associated with Tailapa II in the 10th century.

Prelims focus

  • Krishna I: Kailasa temple at Ellora.
  • Amoghavarsha I: Manyakheta and Kavirajamarga.
  • Indra III: northern campaign against the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Kanauj.
  • Krishna III: Battle of Takkolam, c. 949 CE, against the Cholas.
  • Tripartite struggle: Rashtrakutas, Palas and Gurjara-Pratiharas competed for Kanauj.
  • Trap: Tailapa II replaced Rashtrakuta imperial power around 973 CE; he was not the ruler who founded it.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, printed pp. 20–21; IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 to 1206, BHIC-132, Unit 10, Emergence of Rashtrakutas, printed pp. 153–160, 2019; Historical Outline: List of Rulers over the Chalukyan Territories, Rashtrakuta chronology, Archaeological Survey of India historical publication, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Arrows connect 3 dynasties and their regional bases to contested Kanauj in the Ganga valley, showing they were not all based there.
pictures.caption: The 3 dynasties that contested Kanauj.

title: Major Rashtrakuta Rulers and the Tripartite Struggle for Kanauj

body:
Ellora and the Rashtrakuta period

Ellora is a major rock-cut monument complex in present-day Maharashtra, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, formerly called Aurangabad. Its caves and temples were excavated from the basalt rock of the Deccan plateau over several centuries.

The site is famous for monuments associated with Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism. These monuments belong to different periods. Therefore, Ellora must be understood as a wider religious and artistic centre, not as a group of caves built entirely by one Rashtrakuta ruler.

The most celebrated Rashtrakuta-period achievement at Ellora is the Kailasa or Kailasanatha temple, Cave 16.

Who is associated with Cave 16?

The Kailasa temple at Ellora is traditionally attributed to the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I, who ruled in the later 8th century CE. It is dedicated to Shiva and is among the best-known examples of Indian rock-cut temple architecture.

Ellora, Cave 16: Kailasa or Kailasanatha temple; Krishna I; Shiva; Rashtrakuta period.

Another important Ellora association concerns Dantidurga. An inscription of Dantidurga is connected with Cave 15, also called the Dasavatara cave. This is a separate fact from the attribution of Cave 16 to Krishna I.

Consequently, an inscription associated with Dantidurga at Cave 15 must not be used to identify him as the patron of the Kailasa temple at Cave 16.

What makes the Kailasa temple different?

The most important architectural distinction is that Kailasa is a monolithic rock-cut temple. A monolithic monument is carved from one continuous mass of rock. Unlike an ordinary structural temple, where separate stone blocks are brought together and assembled, the Kailasa temple was created by removing rock from the existing hillside.

Its builders produced the appearance of a large, independent temple complex while keeping the principal monument connected to the original rock mass. The achievement lies in creating a temple with several architectural components through excavation rather than conventional construction from separately laid blocks.

Dravida form and the temple's main features

The Kailasa temple is described as having a Dravida architectural form. This refers to the arrangement and appearance of its temple architecture. It does not mean that the monument was built from separate blocks in the usual manner of structural temples.

The complex includes several recognisable elements:

  • Main Shiva shrine: the principal sacred space of the temple.
  • Vimana: the tower rising above the main shrine. The NCERT description gives its height as approximately 30 metres.
  • Nandi shrine: a separate shrine associated with Nandi, the bull traditionally linked with Shiva.
  • Gateway: an entrance resembling a gopuram, a characteristic gateway form in southern temple architecture.
  • Courtyard, surrounding galleries and subsidiary shrines: parts of the larger temple complex carved from the rock.

The monument therefore combines rock-cut construction with the architectural appearance of a developed Dravida-style temple. These are 2 different characteristics: one describes how the monument was made, while the other describes its architectural form.

Important sculpture at Kailasa

The temple contains large sculptural representations of religious narratives. One especially well-known relief depicts Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa. The sculpture represents a mythological episode in which Ravana attempts to disturb Mount Kailasa, associated with Shiva.

This relief is important as a recognisable artistic feature of the Kailasa temple. The subject of the sculpture should not be confused with the identity of the historical patron: Ravana is a figure represented in the artwork; Krishna I is the Rashtrakuta ruler associated with the temple's construction.

The 3 religious groups of Ellora caves

The Ellora complex is conventionally described as having 34 caves, grouped by their principal religious associations.

Cave numbersPrincipal associationImportant distinction
1–12BuddhistMonastic spaces and Buddhist shrines.
13–29HinduIncludes Cave 15 and the Kailasa temple, Cave 16.
30–34JainJain religious monuments within the same complex.

The coexistence of monuments associated with 3 religious traditions is an important characteristic of Ellora. The Buddhist and Jain monuments are not parts of the Kailasa temple itself; they are separate caves within the larger complex.

Prelims focus

  • Ellora: Maharashtra, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, formerly Aurangabad.
  • Cave 16: Kailasa or Kailasanatha temple, dedicated to Shiva.
  • Krishna I: Rashtrakuta ruler traditionally credited with the Kailasa temple.
  • Cave 15: Dasavatara cave, associated with an inscription of Dantidurga.
  • 34 caves: 1–12 Buddhist, 13–29 Hindu, 30–34 Jain.
  • Trap: Kailasa has a Dravida architectural form but is a monolithic rock-cut monument, not a temple assembled from separate stone blocks.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, printed pp. 41–43, and Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 85–86; Archaeological Survey of India, Ellora Caves, sections on Cave 15 and Cave 16, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ellora Caves, Description and Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 18 November 2026.]
